objectives: Survey family formation + dissolution — marriage, cohabitation, divorce, deinstitutionalization (Cherlin).
Analyze gender, work, and fertility — Goldscheider gender revolution, McDonald gender equity.
Apply register + cohort + assortative-mating methods (Sweden register data, Mare 2011).

slides.title: Family formation + dissolution: Goode + Cherlin + Lillard-Waite
slides.body:
**Social demography** = the study of how social institutions — families, schools, labor markets, neighborhoods, race + class + gender structures — shape demographic processes + outcomes. The family is its central institution: nearly every person's fertility, mortality, migration, and life-course trajectory is mediated by family structure.

**William J. Goode** (*World Revolution and Family Patterns* 1963): the canonical comparative-family study of the postwar era. Goode argued that **industrialization + urbanization + ideology** drive a global convergence toward the **conjugal nuclear family** — partner-chosen, neolocal, child-centered, with reduced kin obligation. Family change happens *unevenly* across regions but in a recognizable direction. Goode's framework dominated comparative family sociology for three decades + has been substantially complicated by empirical work since 1990 (family change in Asia + Africa is much more heterogeneous than convergence predicts; Therborn *Between Sex and Power* 2004 + Cherlin 2009 are critiques).

**Andrew Cherlin** (*The Marriage-Go-Round* 2009; *American Sociological Review* 2004 'The deinstitutionalization of American marriage') — central modern theorist of US family change.
- **Deinstitutionalization of marriage**: marriage is increasingly defined by **personal choice + emotional fulfillment** rather than institutional roles + economic necessity. Marriage rates fall; mean age at first marriage rises; cohabitation diversifies pre-marital + alternative-to-marriage relationships; nonmarital childbearing rises.
- **Marriage-go-round**: Americans churn through relationships at higher rates than Europeans — high marriage, high divorce, high cohabitation, high re-partnering. Children experience more transitions; consequences include behavioral + educational + health impacts (McLanahan + Sandefur 1994 *Growing Up With a Single Parent*; Cherlin + Furstenberg).
- **Diverging destinies** (McLanahan *Demography* 2004): family-structure differences by education widen — college-educated women increasingly delay + have fewer but more stable marriages with planned childbearing; less-educated women experience earlier nonmarital childbearing + family instability. Class divergence in family forms.

**Cohabitation patterns**:
- **Nordic + French model**: cohabitation as long-term equivalent to marriage with children (Sweden, Norway, France). Marriage becomes optional ceremony.
- **Mediterranean / familistic model**: cohabitation remains rare + selective (Italy, Spain pre-2000); now diffusing.
- **US model** (Cherlin): cohabitation as short-term step + frequently unstable.
- **East Asian model** (Japan, Korea, China): cohabitation rare; marriage still strongly normatively linked to childbearing.

**Lillard + Waite** (Lee Lillard + Linda Waite *Demography* 1993, 1995; Waite + Gallagher *The Case for Marriage* 2000): econometric + survey-based work demonstrating that **marriage is associated with better health, longevity, wealth, child outcomes** — controversies remain about selection vs. causation (do healthier people marry, or does marriage cause health). Lillard's hazard-model work (multi-process duration models for marriage + cohabitation + childbearing transitions) is methodologically foundational.

**Divorce**:
- US crude divorce rate peaked ~5.3 per 1000 in 1979-1981 (no-fault divorce laws diffused 1969-1985), now ~2.4. Crude rate is misleading (denominator includes never-married).
- **Refined divorce rate** = divorces / 1000 married women aged 15+. US ~14 (2020). European average ~10. Lowest in religious + South Asian + Middle Eastern societies.
- ~40-45% of US first marriages end in divorce; second + third marriages have higher divorce rates.
- Educational gradient: college-educated US women have divorce rates ~25% vs ~50% for high-school-only.
- **Lillard + Brien + Waite** *Demography* (1995): cohabitation before marriage initially associated with higher divorce risk (selection); the effect has narrowed as cohabitation became more normative.

**Nonmarital childbearing**:
- US: ~40% of births nonmarital (2022); was <10% in 1960.
- Sweden: ~55% of births to non-married mothers (mostly cohabiting partners).
- Concentration by education: among US non-college women, ~60% of first births nonmarital; among college women, ~10%.
- The 'retreat from marriage' as a class phenomenon (Edin + Kefalas *Promises I Can Keep* 2005).

**Multi-state + multi-process demography of the family**:
- **Event-history analysis** + **hazard models** (Lillard, Allison, Hoem): time-to-event models for marriage + cohabitation + childbearing + divorce + dissolution.
- **Multi-process models**: jointly estimate fertility + marriage + cohabitation hazards with shared unobserved heterogeneity (Lillard).
- **Stationary equivalent** + **synthetic-cohort** measures: total first-marriage rate, total divorce rate, mean expected duration of cohabitation.

slides.title: Gender, work, fertility: Goldscheider + McDonald + Esping-Andersen
slides.body:
**Gender** is the single most consequential axis of social variation in modern fertility decisions. Three frameworks dominate.

**Frances Goldscheider + Eva Bernhardt + Trude Lappegård** (*Population and Development Review* 2015) — **Gender Revolution in two halves**:
- **First half** (~1960-1990 in HICs): women enter public sphere (education, employment). Removes one barrier to economic independence; sharply *lowers* fertility because women's opportunity cost rises + work-family conflict intensifies.
- **Second half** (~1990-): men enter private sphere (housework, childcare). When gender equity in domestic work catches up, work-family conflict eases + fertility may stabilize or recover.
- **U-shaped curve hypothesis**: TFR falls during the first half + recovers in the second half as both spheres approach equity.
- **Empirical patterns** (Esping-Andersen *The Incomplete Revolution* 2009; Goldscheider + Bernhardt + Lappegård 2015):
  - Nordic countries (Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Denmark): furthest along the second half. TFR ~1.6-1.9 (Sweden + Norway have slipped recently but historically were ~2.0).
  - Anglo-Saxon (US, UK, Australia, NZ): moderate progress; TFR ~1.5-1.8.
  - Continental (Germany, France, Belgium, Netherlands): variable; France high (~1.8) via family policy.
  - Mediterranean (Italy, Spain, Greece, Portugal): first half advanced (women's education + employment) but second half lagging (male housework + childcare share low); lowest-low TFR.
  - East Asian (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong): most extreme — first half far advanced, second half barely started; TFR 0.78-1.4 (Korea lowest national TFR ever).

**Peter McDonald** (*Population and Development Review* 2000, 2013) — **Gender-equity hypothesis**: 'Below-replacement fertility persists where gender equity in *individual-oriented* institutions (education, employment, civil rights) is high but equity in *family-oriented* institutions (marriage, household, parenting) is low.' Korea + Italy + Japan canonical cases. Predicts: family-friendly policy (parental leave, childcare, fathers' use of leave) can shift the equilibrium.

**Gøsta Esping-Andersen** (*The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism* 1990; *The Incomplete Revolution* 2009): welfare-state regimes shape gender + family arrangements. **Social-democratic** (Nordic) regimes most supportive of dual-earner families with state-provided childcare; **conservative** (continental Europe) regimes support male-breadwinner families; **liberal** (Anglo-Saxon) regimes minimal support; **familistic** (Mediterranean, East Asian) regimes rely on extended family. Predicts cross-regime fertility differences.

**Dual-earner family + the work-family squeeze**:
- Female labor-force participation rose dramatically across HICs from ~30% (1960) to ~70-80% (2020).
- Mean weekly work hours in households with children rose; sleep + leisure fell.
- **Time-use studies** (Hochschild *The Second Shift* 1989; Bianchi + Robinson + Milkie *Changing Rhythms of American Family Life* 2006): women's paid + unpaid work combined often exceeds men's; the 'second shift' of domestic labor disproportionately on women.
- **Intensive parenting** norms (Hays *The Cultural Contradictions of Motherhood* 1996; Lareau *Unequal Childhoods* 2003): rising time + emotional investment expected per child; raises perceived cost of additional children.
- **Stalled gender revolution** (England 2010 *Gender + Society*): progress in education + occupation slowed; housework gap narrowed only partially; second shift persists.

**Empirical implications**:
- TFR correlates *negatively* with female labor-force participation cross-sectionally + within countries pre-2000.
- After ~2000, the correlation reversed in HICs: countries with higher FLFP now have *higher* TFR (Nordic + Anglo > Mediterranean + East Asian) — consistent with the gender-revolution + second-half hypothesis.
- **Childcare availability + cost** is a strong predictor of completed fertility (Adsera; Hilgeman + Butts).
- **Parental-leave policy** — generosity, paternal share, flexibility — predicts both maternal labor-force return + fertility recovery (Brewster + Rindfuss 2000).
- **Housing affordability** is a strong fertility constraint in East Asia + parts of Europe + the US — first-birth postponement amplified by housing costs.

**Gender + life course**:
- Mean age at first birth in HICs: from ~21-23 (1960-1970) to ~28-32 (2020).
- Postponement compresses the reproductive window; raises infertility incidence; drives demand for assisted reproductive technology (~2% of births in HICs).
- **Cohort vs period TFR divergence** is largely a postponement story (Bongaarts-Feeney 1998 tempo adjustment).

**Gender + mortality**:
- Female advantage in life expectancy: 4-7 years globally; declined in some HICs as women's smoking + work-stress patterns converged with men's; rose in post-Soviet states with male mortality crisis.
- US gender mortality gap has narrowed since 1980 to ~5 years (down from ~7 years).

slides.title: Intergenerational + register data + assortative mating: Mare + Sweden + Mass Demography
slides.body:
**Intergenerational demography** = the study of how demographic + social outcomes are transmitted across generations. Modern register + longitudinal microdata have transformed the field.

**Robert Mare** (*Annual Review of Sociology* 1991, *Demography* 2011 Presidential Address 'A multigenerational view of inequality') — argued sociology + demography must move beyond two-generation parent-child models to **multigenerational** (grandparent + grandchild + lateral kin) studies. Three reasons:
1. **Grandparent effects** on grandchildren (independent of parent — Knigge 2016; Pfeffer 2014).
2. **Multigenerational inequality persistence** is greater than two-generation models suggest (Clark *The Son Also Rises* 2014; Solon).
3. **Demographic + assortative mating** mechanisms compound inequality across generations.

**Mass Demography** + **Mare's multigenerational models**:
- Use **kinship-network** projections (SOCSIM, Mason).
- Incorporate **assortative mating** + **fertility differences** by social class to model how inequality propagates.
- Show that completed-fertility differences (poor higher TFR than rich in HICs) systematically shift composition over generations.

**Assortative mating**:
- **Educational homogamy**: share of married couples with both partners college-educated rose from ~5% (1960) to ~20-25% (2020) in US; from ~3% to ~25% in Europe (Schwartz + Mare *Demography* 2005; Eika + Mogstad + Zafar *JPE* 2019; Greenwood + Guner 2014).
- **Earnings homogamy**: rose substantially in US 1960-2010; ~33% of inter-household income inequality is attributable to assortative mating (Greenwood + Guner + Kocharkov + Santos 2014; Eika et al. 2019).
- **Educational assortative mating + intergenerational mobility**: higher homogamy concentrates resources + reduces mobility (cross-references Becker; Fernández + Rogerson).

**Sweden register data + Nordic linked administrative records**:
- Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Netherlands maintain population registers with **link-able microdata** across census, vital events, income, education, parental, sibling, kinship records covering decades.
- **Black + Devereux + Salvanes** (2005 *AER* Norway); **Lindahl + Palme + Sandgren + Sjögren** (Sweden multigenerational); **Modin + Erikson + Vågerö** Sweden; **van Bavel + Gabrielli** Belgium.
- Enable: sibling fixed-effect models, twin studies, multi-generational mobility, intergenerational mortality + fertility transmission, neighborhood + school effects on outcomes.
- Considered the **gold standard** for causal-identification + intergenerational demography. The combination of dense administrative coverage + long historical records is unique to the Nordic + Netherlands setting; partially emulated by US tax-record-based work (Chetty + Hendren *QJE* 2014, 2018).
- **HFD** (Human Fertility Database) draws heavily on register data for cohort fertility metrics.

**Empirical findings from register + longitudinal data**:
- **Intergenerational fertility transmission**: ~0.2-0.3 correlation parent-child completed fertility (Murphy + Knudsen 2002; Kolk 2014); cultural + genetic + structural channels mixed.
- **Sibling effects on family formation**: older sister having a child raises probability of younger sister having a child within 2 years (Lyngstad + Prskawetz 2010 Norway).
- **Intergenerational longevity**: ~0.2-0.3 correlation parent-child $e_x$ at older ages (Mitchell + Hsueh + King 2001).
- **Intergenerational mobility**: Chetty et al. *QJE* 2014 — US rank-rank slope ~0.34; Scandinavian countries 0.18-0.25 (more mobile).

**Pew Family Change Reports** (Pew Research Center): regular comparative reports on US + global family change. Recent topics:
- Rising share of US adults never married (~25% of 40-year-olds, up from ~6% in 1970).
- Decline in marriage among Black Americans + working-class whites.
- Cohabitation + cohabitation with children.
- Multigenerational households.

**Family demography in non-Western contexts**:
- **Therborn** (*Between Sex and Power* 2004) — global comparative family systems: Western, Eastern (Confucian + Japanese), Indian, sub-Saharan African, Islamic. Each has distinct trajectories; Goode's convergence is partial at best.
- **South Asia**: arranged marriage persists strongly; rising age at marriage + lowest dowry effects (Anukriti, Karthikeyan).
- **Sub-Saharan Africa**: polygyny, kin fostering, extended-family residence; fertility transition slower than predicted.
- **East Asia**: marriage still strongly normatively linked to childbearing; family change slower than fertility decline → growing share never married + childless.

Next: lesson 8 develops the computational + AI + algorithmic frontier including agent-based models + machine-learning fertility-mortality + digital trace data + LLM-augmented projection.

question.question: Apply Goldscheider gender revolution + McDonald gender equity to a low-fertility society
question.goal: Diagnose Korea's TFR 0.78 (2022) through the Goldscheider two-halves + McDonald equity-incongruence frameworks.

steps.prompt: Korea's first-half progress — what does it look like?

acceptedAnswers: very high female educational attainment, rising labor force participation, women out-perform men in tertiary education

steps.reveal: Korea's first-half gender revolution is far advanced: female tertiary education attainment ~76% (highest among OECD); women now exceed men in university enrollment. Female labor-force participation ~60% (rising). Korea has substantial gender equity in formal education + labor-market access — at least at entry. The first half (women entering public sphere) is largely complete.

acceptedAnswers: very limited male participation in housework and childcare; persistent gender wage gap; motherhood penalty; long working hours culture

steps.reveal: Second half is barely started: Korean men's share of housework + childcare among the lowest in OECD (~50 min/day vs ~3-4 hours for women). Gender wage gap ~31% (highest in OECD). Motherhood penalty: Korean women's employment drops sharply after childbirth + return rates are low. Long-hours work culture + intensive 'tiger mom' parenting norms compound work-family conflict. McDonald gender-equity hypothesis: this incongruence (public-sphere equity high + private-sphere equity low) drives below-replacement persistence. Korea is McDonald's textbook case.

steps.prompt: What policy levers does McDonald suggest + which has Korea tried?

acceptedAnswers: paternal leave, public childcare, work-hour reduction, gender-equity-in-family campaigns; Korea has tried subsidies and paternal leave with limited uptake

steps.reveal: McDonald: make second-half progress easier. Levers: paid paternal leave (with high replacement + non-transferable to mother); affordable + accessible public childcare; statutory work-hour caps; gender-equity-in-housework normative campaigns + role models. Korea has expanded parental leave (12 months, both parents) + subsidies for newborns (KRW 10 M+ baby bonus) + housing support, but uptake is low (paternal leave taken by ~5-10% of fathers; cultural norms + workplace penalties remain). France + Sweden have had more sustained effect with higher generosity + longer-running normative shifts.

steps.prompt: What does Goldscheider predict for Korea's fertility trajectory?

acceptedAnswers: U-shape recovery is theoretically possible if second-half gender revolution progresses, but Korea is far from that point and Lutz low-fertility trap may operate

steps.reveal: Goldscheider + Bernhardt + Lappegård (2015): TFR can recover toward 1.7-2.0 if the second-half gender revolution progresses substantially. Sweden + Norway provide the model. But Korea is far from that — male housework + childcare share among lowest, work-hours culture intense, housing costs prohibitive. **Lutz low-fertility trap** plausibly operating: shrinking cohorts of parents, declining youth labor force, normative shift toward small / no children. Korea is the limit case of the open question: does the second half come fast enough to recover fertility, or does the trap close?

question.question: Why is Andrew Cherlin's *deinstitutionalization of marriage* thesis (2004, 2009) a foundational frame for US family demography?
options: Cherlin (*Journal of Marriage and Family* 2004; *The Marriage-Go-Round* 2009) argued marriage in the US has shifted from an **institutional** form (clear, taken-for-granted roles + economic + religious bases) toward a **personal-choice** form structured by emotional fulfillment + relationship work. Consequences: (1) declining marriage rates + rising age at first marriage; (2) rising cohabitation (often unstable + short-term in the US); (3) rising nonmarital childbearing (~40% of US births in 2022); (4) high divorce + remarriage rates ('marriage-go-round'); (5) **diverging destinies** (McLanahan 2004) — college-educated women increasingly delay marriage + childbearing into stable + planned arrangements; less-educated women experience earlier + more unstable family forms. The class divergence in family structures is now one of the most consequential demographic stratifications, with major effects on children's outcomes (educational, behavioral, economic). Cherlin's thesis reframed US family demography away from convergence-toward-conjugal-nuclear-family (Goode 1963) toward stratified + churning + class-divergent forms.
question.explanation: Cherlin (2004, 2009) — deinstitutionalization of marriage: shift from institutional to personal-choice form → declining marriage rates, rising cohabitation, ~40% US nonmarital births, marriage-go-round of high divorce + re-partnering, McLanahan's diverging destinies by education. Reframed US family demography away from Goode's convergence thesis toward class-divergent + churning forms.

slides.workedSolution: Cherlin (2004, 2009) deinstitutionalization: marriage shifted from institutional form to personal-choice form → declining rates, rising cohabitation, ~40% US nonmarital births, high churn. McLanahan's diverging destinies by education widens class gap in family forms. Reframed US family demography away from Goode's convergence thesis.

question.question: Designing a multigenerational study using Swedish register data
question.prompt: You have access to Swedish linked administrative microdata covering 1970-2020 (population register + tax + education + parental + sibling links). In ≤200 words, design a study examining intergenerational fertility transmission with **Mare's multigenerational** framing. Cover: (a) what variables you'd use to test grandparent effects on grandchild fertility independent of parent effects; (b) how you'd model **assortative mating** in the parent generation (educational homogamy from Schwartz + Mare 2005); (c) two threats to causal identification (selection, omitted variables); (d) why the Swedish register context is methodologically privileged (Black + Devereux + Salvanes; Lindahl-Palme-Sandgren-Sjögren); (e) one practical analytic model (linear mixed-effects with kinship random effects, hazard model for first birth, Lillard-style multi-process). Name one comparison dataset (Norway MoBa, Netherlands LISS, US PSID) to triangulate.

question.question: If the parent-child correlation in completed fertility is $\rho = 0.25$ + the variance of children-per-woman in the parent generation is $\sigma^2 = 1.0$, the expected predicted change in mean fertility per cohort due to assortative + transmission processes (Becker-style simplified) is approximately $\rho \sigma$. Compute it (children per cohort per woman).
question.hint: $\rho \sigma = 0.25 \times 1.0 = 0.25$ — i.e., if mean fertility in the parent generation is 1 child above population mean, expected child fertility is ~0.25 above mean. Demonstrates the **transmission slope** in completed fertility ~0.2-0.3 documented by Murphy-Knudsen, Kolk + others; relatively modest but compounded across generations as in Mare's multigenerational framing.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain how social demography frames family + gender + intergenerational change. Cover (a) family formation + dissolution (Goode, Cherlin deinstitutionalization, Lillard-Waite hazard models, divorce + nonmarital childbearing); (b) gender + work + fertility (Goldscheider gender revolution two halves, McDonald gender equity, Esping-Andersen welfare regimes, dual earner + intensive parenting); (c) intergenerational (Mare 2011 multigenerational, Sweden register data, assortative mating Schwartz-Mare, Pew family-change reports).
question.rubric: Mentions: Goode (*World Revolution and Family Patterns* 1963) — convergence toward conjugal nuclear family + later critiques. Cherlin (2004, 2009) — deinstitutionalization of marriage, marriage-go-round, McLanahan diverging destinies. Lillard-Waite hazard + multi-process models. Divorce + nonmarital childbearing ~40% US. Goldscheider + Bernhardt + Lappegård (2015) — gender revolution in two halves: first lowers fertility, second may stabilize. McDonald (2000, 2013) — gender-equity incongruence drives lowest-low fertility. Esping-Andersen welfare regimes. Mare (2011) — multigenerational inequality + grandparent effects. Sweden + Nordic register data — gold standard for causal identification of intergenerational transmission. Schwartz + Mare (2005) educational assortative mating. Pew family change reports. Concludes: social demography unifies family + gender + class + cohort + intergenerational lenses on the institutional context of fertility + mortality + migration.
